extracted.intended_audience: photographers, photojournalists, critics, students and readers interested in documentary photography ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical questions for judging documentary/photojournalistic images of suffering — focusing on ethics, representation, captions, authorial stance, and the emotional/social consequences of images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do photographs trigger action (not just empathy)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the photograph contribute to the sort of empathic feeling that triggers action — does it matter if we cry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that empathy alone is not enough; evaluate whether images move viewers toward action or leave them in passive feeling. Consider whether emotional response generated (pity, guilt, shame) motivates interventions or simply aestheticizes suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial commitment and empathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the author's commitment to the work and empathy toward subjects evident (i.e., is the work humanistic)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commitment/empathy are positive markers but not sufficient. Assess whether the photographer's compassion translates into responsible representation rather than aestheticizing or simplifying subjects' lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualization and specificity of subject lives
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work account for the lives depicted, for particular stories and social environments, or does it paint realities impressionistically (blurred and beautified)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer photos and accompanying text that provide concrete context (who, where, why) over images that treat people as generic types. The page warns against reducing complex social realities to impressionistic compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beautifying the ugly / inauthenticity of the beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs that depict suffering shouldn't be beautiful, as beauty can drain attention from the sobering subject and turn it toward the medium itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sontag's critique: beauty may compromise a picture's status as a document by making suffering a spectacle. When judging work, note when aesthetic form distracts from or softens the reality shown (examples: composed 'beautiful' shots that obscure humanitarian reality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions should not moralize; name subjects when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions shouldn't moralize, and failing to name the powerless in captions demotes them to representative instances rather than persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post quotes Sontag: 'A portrait that declines to name its subject becomes complicit...'; evaluate captions for naming, specificity, avoidance of moralizing language, and whether they restore subject agency and identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle versus sober documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the image make the spectacular not spectacular (or vice versa)? Is the spectacle part of religious/narrative forms that risk turning suffering into spectacle?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the photographer attempts to neutralize spectacle (making the spectacular 'not spectacular') and whether that succeeds ethically. Beware images that unintentionally foreground spectacle and emotional shock value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional outcomes: inspiration for justice vs guilt/despondency
rubrics_metrics.description: Do images inspire social justice and hope, or do they produce a subconscious default to guilt, despondency and powerlessness in viewers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reviewers' observations (e.g., Pete Brook on Nachtwey) to assess the downstream emotional effects of images. Strong work should be evaluated on whether it mobilizes concern into action rather than only prompting voyeuristic guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about authorial presence and style
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming to be an absent messenger is naïf; the photographer's style and choices shape meaning and should be acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether photographers are transparent about their aesthetic choices and their positionality. Pretending neutrality while using a recognizable style can mislead viewers about the image's documentary status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing people to compositional elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There's a risk of turning people into points and lines inside a frame instead of naming them and conveying personhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique images that treat bodies as compositional devices (e.g., arranging nameless corpses as visual forms). Prefer images that restore individuality and context rather than abstracting people for visual effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey witness experience and felt context
rubrics_metrics.description: For those who haven't seen tragedies, it's important to understand the moment witnessed by the photographer — how he felt death — not just how nameless bodies fit into one picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the photograph and accompanying material communicate the photographer's witnessed experience and situational context, helping viewers grasp lived reality rather than ingesting a detached aesthetic.
